subject: The 5 numbers that decide every rental deal (in 60 seconds)
preheader: Cap rate, cash-on-cash, DSCR, monthly NCF, 10-yr IRR — and which to weight when

marketSnapshot.headline: Five numbers decide whether a rental deal pencils
marketSnapshot.body: Serious investors run the same 5-number triage on every deal before committing real time. Cap rate, cash-on-cash return, DSCR, monthly net cash flow, and projected 10-year IRR each answer a different question. Use them to prioritize deeper review, then compare asking with the target-dependent Offer Ceiling and verify rent, financing, taxes, insurance, condition, and material costs before deciding or negotiating.

dealSpotter.body: $245k 3/2 at $1,950 rent. Cap rate 7.9%, cash-on-cash 11.4% with 25% down, DSCR 1.31, monthly net cash flow $735, projected 10-yr IRR 13.8%. Every metric clears the threshold for its class. This is the kind of deal that compounds reliably — boring, not exciting, and worth pursuing fast when you find one.

dealSpotter.headlineNumber: Cap weak, IRR strong — appreciation play
dealSpotter.body: $485k 2-unit at $4,300/mo gross. Cap rate 5.6% (weak by yield standards), cash-on-cash 6.2%, DSCR 1.18 (tight). But projected 10-yr IRR is 14%+ once you factor neighborhood appreciation tailwind. The 5-number triage flags this as a deliberate bet — you're trading current yield for future appreciation. Valid choice IF you can hold long enough and have the cash flow elsewhere to fund the tight current month.

$245k 3-unit at $3,600/mo gross. Cap rate 9.5% on paper. The trap: at investor-loan rates with realistic vacancy + capex, DSCR drops to 1.04 — below most lender funding thresholds. Cash-on-cash actually negative once you put down enough to clear the lender's DSCR. The 5-number triage caught what the listing's headline cap rate hid.

blogFeature.title: Cap rate vs cash-on-cash vs DSCR — which metric actually matters?
blogFeature.excerpt: Three different metrics, three different questions they answer. Why most investors quote cap rate when they should be looking at cash-on-cash, and why your lender cares only about DSCR.

qa.question: Which of the 5 numbers should I weight most heavily?
qa.answer: Depends on your goal. If you need cash flow to supplement income, weight monthly net cash flow and cash-on-cash — those answer 'will this property pay me reliably each month?' If you're building wealth and don't need the rental income, weight projected 10-year IRR — that answers 'will my equity compound efficiently?' DSCR is the constraint metric, not the goal metric — it just has to clear your lender's floor (typically 1.20-1.25) for the deal to be financeable. Cap rate is mainly useful for comparing across deals in the same market, not as a hard threshold. The best mental model: cash-on-cash and monthly NCF for income investors, IRR for wealth-builders, DSCR for everyone as a constraint.
